scenes.headline: 4 MARKETS, 0 POOLING
scenes.subtext: Without postponement, every country buffers alone.
scenes.spoken: You sell one product in four countries — Switzerland, Germany, Great Britain, and Italy. Each market gets its own variant. Without postponement, your supply chain treats every variant as a completely separate product. That means four independent safety stocks, four separate orders — and four times the cost.

scenes.headline: EACH VARIANT = OWN PRODUCT
scenes.subtext: Same newsvendor formula, four times over.
scenes.spoken: The setup: lead time is six weeks, holding cost is five francs per unit per week, and penalty cost for stockouts is ninety-five francs. Calculate the critical ratio first: CR equals H divided by H plus P — that gives you five over one hundred, or five percent. Look up the Z-value and the F-value from the standard normal table. You need both for the formulas ahead.

scenes.headline: CV REVEALS THE RISK
scenes.subtext: Coefficient of variance: σ divided by μ.
scenes.spoken: Before you calculate anything, compare the markets. Do not just look at the raw standard deviation — divide it by the mean to get the coefficient of variance. Switzerland and Germany have high CV — demand is highly variable relative to the mean. Great Britain and Italy have low CV — demand is much more stable. High CV means higher safety stock, higher cost.

scenes.headline: EXCEL TIP: NAME YOUR CELLS
scenes.subtext: LT, H, P, CR, Z, F — no magic numbers.
scenes.spoken: Here is an exam tip that saves time and prevents errors. In Excel, name your parameter cells: call E4 LT for lead time, E5 H for holding cost, E6 P for penalty cost. Then name the derived values CR, Z, and F. Now your formulas read like the textbook — no cryptic cell addresses, no wrong references. Just type LT, H, Z directly.

scenes.headline: ORDER QUANTITY FORMULA
scenes.subtext: Optimal Q* per country — Newsvendor extended with lead time.
scenes.spoken: The optimal order quantity for each country extends the newsvendor formula with lead time. Q-star equals LT plus one multiplied by the expected weekly demand, plus Z times sigma times the square root of LT plus one. In Excel for Switzerland: equals LT plus one times mu, plus Z times sigma times SQRT of LT plus one. Copy the formula down for Germany, Great Britain, and Italy.

scenes.headline: COST FORMULA PER COUNTRY
scenes.subtext: Expected cost for each country configuration.
scenes.spoken: The expected cost for each configuration: H plus P times F times sigma times square root of LT plus one. In Excel: equals H plus P times F times sigma times SQRT of LT plus one. Copy down for all four countries. Then sum the order quantities and sum the costs. These totals are your baseline — the cost of running the supply chain WITHOUT pooling.

scenes.headline: THIS IS YOUR BASELINE
scenes.subtext: Next: postponement cuts this cost by pooling stock.
scenes.spoken: Four separate safety stocks mean four times the insurance against demand uncertainty. The total cost you just calculated is the without-postponement baseline. In the next video, postponement pools all four variants into one stock, reducing total safety stock dramatically — because the variances partially cancel out. Remember the formula, remember CV, and name your cells in Excel. That's supply chain without postponement.

title: Supply Chain without Postponement — OM HSG
